name: Venlafaxine
short: SNRI whose NET inhibition grows with dose; CYP2D6 converts it to desvenlafaxine.
mechanism: Inhibits **SERT** potently even at low doses and **NET** with moderate potency, robustly only at **higher doses**; no significant other receptor actions. **CYP2D6** converts it to **desvenlafaxine**, normally about twice the plasma level of parent drug.
uses: Unipolar depression; efficacy often rises with dose (noradrenergic boost)

sideEffects.e: Bothersome **withdrawal**, especially after high-dose long-term use
Nausea, worse with the IR form

facts.text: 2D6 inhibitors and **poor metabolizers** shift the ratio toward parent venlafaxine, reducing NET inhibition: how much NET inhibition a dose gives is **unpredictable**. The XR form is a considerable improvement over IR.

Boosts descending **NE and 5HT** inhibition in the dorsal horn, so irrelevant input from joints, muscles and gut is ignored again; treats pain across the spectrum from depression to fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathy, low back pain and osteoarthritis.
Has NET-inhibiting actions and has been used for ADHD with varying success; only atomoxetine is approved.

name: Desvenlafaxine
short: Active metabolite of venlafaxine with more consistent NET inhibition.
mechanism: Inhibits **SERT and NET**, with **more NET relative to SERT** than venlafaxine but still more potent at SERT. As a separate drug it gives more consistent NET inhibition across patients.

facts.text: Less need for dose titration than venlafaxine because NET inhibition does not depend on CYP2D6 conversion.

Boosts descending **NE and 5HT** inhibition in the dorsal horn, so irrelevant input from joints, muscles and gut is ignored again; treats pain across the spectrum from depression to fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathy, low back pain and osteoarthritis.
Has NET-inhibiting actions and has been used for ADHD with varying success; only atomoxetine is approved.

name: Duloxetine
short: SNRI that treats depression, pain and painful physical symptoms.
mechanism: Inhibits **SERT slightly more potently than NET**. NET inhibition seems critical for pain relief and, via raised PFC NE and DA, for cognitive symptoms.
uses: Diabetic peripheral **neuropathic pain**, **fibromyalgia**, chronic **musculoskeletal pain** (osteoarthritis, low back)

facts.text: Showed that somatic pain is a legitimate symptom of depression. Usually started **twice daily**; once daily after tolerance. Less hypertension and milder withdrawal than venlafaxine.

Boosts descending **NE and 5HT** inhibition in the dorsal horn, so irrelevant input from joints, muscles and gut is ignored again; treats pain across the spectrum from depression to fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathy, low back pain and osteoarthritis.
Has NET-inhibiting actions and has been used for ADHD with varying success; only atomoxetine is approved.

name: Milnacipran
short: SNRI that is more potent at NET than SERT; for fibromyalgia in the US.
mechanism: A racemic SNRI that is **more potent at NET than SERT**, unlike venlafaxine and duloxetine. The S (levo) enantiomer is the active one.
uses: Possibly painful physical symptoms, neuropathic pain and cognitive symptoms (“**fibro-fog**”)

facts.text: The first SNRI in Japan and many European countries. Needs **twice-daily** dosing (short half-life). An α1 antagonist relieves urinary hesitancy.

Boosts descending **NE and 5HT** inhibition in the dorsal horn, so irrelevant input from joints, muscles and gut is ignored again; treats pain across the spectrum from depression to fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathy, low back pain and osteoarthritis.
Potent NET binding at **all** clinically effective doses may make it especially useful for **fibro-fog**.
Has NET-inhibiting actions and has been used for ADHD with varying success; only atomoxetine is approved.

name: Levomilnacipran
short: The active S enantiomer of milnacipran; once-daily SNRI for MDD.
mechanism: The active **S enantiomer** of milnacipran, with **greater NET than SERT** inhibition, in a controlled-release once-daily form.
uses: Unipolar major depressive disorder (US); may target **fatigue and low energy**

facts.text: Unlike racemic milnacipran it is given **once daily**.

Boosts descending **NE and 5HT** inhibition in the dorsal horn, so irrelevant input from joints, muscles and gut is ignored again; treats pain across the spectrum from depression to fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathy, low back pain and osteoarthritis.
Potent NET binding at **all** clinically effective doses may make it especially useful for **fibro-fog**.

name: Bupropion
short: NDRI with low, slow DAT occupancy; activating, no sexual dysfunction.
mechanism: Weakly inhibits **DAT** and **NET**; active metabolites (most potently **radafaxine**, the + enantiomer of 6-hydroxy-bupropion) are more potent at NET, equally potent at DAT and concentrated in brain. PET shows only **10–30%** striatal DAT occupancy: **low, slow and long-lasting**, enough to help without abuse. Also a **CYP2D6 inhibitor**.
uses: Unipolar depression, especially **reduced positive affect** (“dopamine deficiency syndrome”)
Augmenting or replacing SSRIs/SNRIs (residual or drug-induced low energy, interest)
With **dextromethorphan**: depression and Alzheimer agitation (in trials at publication)

sideEffects.e: **Seizures** at peak plasma levels (reduced by SR and XL)

facts.text: IR (three times daily) → SR (twice daily) → **XL** (once daily); IR is all but abandoned.
SSRI or SNRI + bupropion = **triple-action** combination, among the most popular in the US.
Used for ancillary symptoms of **fibromyalgia** (see Chapter 9 table).
Has NET-inhibiting actions and has been used for ADHD with varying success; only atomoxetine is approved.
An **NDRI**: weak NET plus weak DAT inhibition, so unlike atomoxetine it also reaches accumbens DATs (Figure 11-37).
Boosts dextromethorphan via **CYP2D6** inhibition for AD agitation; also suggested for **apathy** as a pro-dopaminergic agent.
For smoking cessation, returns a little dopamine to craving accumbens D2 receptors; quit rate about **half** that of varenicline.

updates.title: Combined with dextromethorphan for depression
updates.text: **Dextromethorphan–bupropion** (Auvelity) was approved for major depressive disorder in adults in August 2022, and for agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia in April 2026.

name: Agomelatine
nbn: Melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist and serotonin 5HT2C receptor antagonist
short: MT1/MT2 agonist and 5HT2C/5HT2B antagonist that may reset circadian rhythms.
mechanism: An **MT1/MT2 agonist** (“substitute melatonin” in the SCN) and a **5HT2C** and 5HT2B **antagonist**. 5HT2C blockade disinhibits **NE and DA** release in the PFC; combined SCN actions may **resynchronize** circadian rhythms and reverse the phase delay of depression.

facts.text: Melatonin and 5HT2C receptors in the SCN are expressed most at night; agomelatine acts on both to reset rhythms (Figure 7-39).
Also an MT1/MT2 agonist acting on circadian rhythms (Figure 10-57).

name: Mirtazapine
short: α2 antagonist that also blocks 5HT2A, 5HT2C, 5HT3 and H1; blocks no transporter.
mechanism: Blocks **no monoamine transporter**. **α2 antagonism** disinhibits both **NE** (autoreceptors) and **5HT** (heteroreceptors) release; **5HT2A** and **5HT2C** antagonism release DA and NE in the PFC and improve sleep; **5HT3** antagonism disinhibits glutamate, ACh and NE; **H1** antagonism sedates.
uses: With an **SNRI** (“**California rocket fuel**”) for nonresponse to an SNRI alone

facts.text: A **5HT3 antagonist** with pro-cognitive and antidepressant actions (Table 3-2).
Combined **H1 + 5HT2C** antagonism links it to weight gain; asenapine is structurally related and shares several of its binding properties.
Five principal actions: **α2, 5HT2A, 5HT2C, 5HT3 and H1** antagonism. α2 antagonism gives a dual 5HT–NE action like an SNRI’s by a different mechanism, synergistic with reuptake blockade.
Off-label option for **GAD** and for **panic attacks**.
Used for ancillary symptoms of **fibromyalgia** (see Chapter 9 table).
Sedating via H1 (with other) blockade; mirtazapine and chlorpromazine fall in the “still too hot” (hangover) category of Figure 10-41C.

nbn: Norepinephrine and serotonin receptor antagonist (α2, 5HT2A, 5HT2C, 5HT3, H1)

name: Mianserin
nbn: Norepinephrine receptor antagonist (α2, α1) with 5HT2A, 5HT2C, 5HT3 and H1 antagonism
short: Mirtazapine-like α2 antagonist with added α1 blockade; not in the US.
mechanism: Like mirtazapine (**α2, 5HT2A, 5HT2C, 5HT3, H1** antagonism) but with potent **α1 antagonism**, which mitigates serotonergic enhancement, so it boosts mainly **noradrenergic** transmission.

facts.text: Another α2 antagonist, **setiptiline**, is marketed in Japan.

name: Trazodone
nbn: Serotonin receptor antagonist (5HT2A/2C) and reuptake inhibitor
short: SARI: a hypnotic at low doses and an antidepressant at high doses.
mechanism: Blocks **5HT2A** and **5HT2C** receptors and **SERT**, plus 5HT1D, 5HT2B, 5HT7, **α1A/α1B**, α2B/α2C and **H1** receptors, with **5HT1A agonism**. Low doses engage only the highest-affinity targets (5HT2A, α1, H1: **hypnotic**); 150–600 mg saturates SERT and recruits the rest (**antidepressant**).
uses: **Insomnia**, especially residual insomnia after SSRIs/SNRIs (25–150 mg, immediate release)
Unipolar depression (150–600 mg; once-nightly **XR** reduces daytime sedation)

sideEffects.e: Daytime **sedation** at peak levels with IR antidepressant dosing
No sexual dysfunction or weight gain; less insomnia and anxiety than SSRIs

facts.text: Bars follow the affinity (Ki) ranking in **Figure 7-45**, highest to lowest; actions beyond those named in the text are shown as “binds.”
300 mg **XR** once nightly gives levels that never fall below the antidepressant minimum, with a peak similar to 100 mg IR (Figure 7-47).
Off-label option for **GAD** and for **panic attacks**.
Used for ancillary symptoms of **fibromyalgia** (see Chapter 9 table).
The **most commonly prescribed** sleep agent worldwide (not approved for insomnia); reduces arousal by blocking 5HT2A, α1 and H1; no tolerance, withdrawal, dependence or rebound.
In dementia, low-dose nightly trazodone (half-life **6–8 h**) improves sleep without daytime effects; may help behavior in **FTD** more than AD.

name: Nefazodone
nbn: Serotonin receptor antagonist (5HT2A) and reuptake inhibitor
short: SARI with robust 5HT2A antagonism; rarely used because of liver toxicity.
mechanism: Robust **5HT2A** antagonism with weaker **5HT2C** antagonism and **SERT** inhibition; its icon also shows **NET** inhibition and **α1** antagonism.
